g.aria-label: Kawliya (Iraq): community reference; horse word unverified
g.title: No modern Iraqi Kawliya-specific word for horse has been verified. The open marker records documented community presence only and is not assigned a horse-word origin colour. Newbold (1856) recorded asp from a Duman informant from Altun Kupri; that historical northern Iraqi record is not substituted for present-day Kawliya speech in southern Iraq. Iraqi communities have varied language practices and identities.

g.aria-label: Flemish Dutch regional forms: peerd / peird
Domari (Aleppo word; Damascus community reference): agōra
Domari (Aleppo word; Damascus community reference): agōra

g.title: The displayed modern word each is Scottish Gaelic. Its ancestor *ekʷos is reconstructed Proto-Celtic, not a Scottish Gaelic word: PIE *h₁éḱwos → Proto-Celtic *ekʷos → Old Irish ech → Scottish Gaelic each.

PIE *h₁éḱwos → Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćwas → Proto-Iranian *Hácwah → the selected asp/asb/hesp forms. Individual histories include Iranian-internal borrowing. Gilaki, Iranian Talysh and Mazandarani asb are separately documented regional forms. The shared origin colour does not imply that each selected form has an uninterrupted inheritance history: Iranian-internal borrowing is possible.
PIE *h₁éḱwos → Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos) → learned Modern Greek ίππος. This coexists with everyday άλογο, which has a separate origin.

The caballus / *kaballos word-family is shown under one shared heading with three separately coloured routes. Romance words continue Latin caballus; Albanian kalë is borrowed through Latin. Irish capall, Manx cabbyl and Welsh ceffyl belong to the related Celtic word-family, with disputed early borrowing directions and deeper origin. The shared heading does not assert that every Celtic term descends directly from Latin. This family is distinct from Latin equus, the inherited PIE horse noun.
Latin caballus → the Romance horse words shown here, including Spanish caballo, French cheval and Italian cavallo.

The related caballos word-family in Celtic: Irish capall, Manx cabbyl and Welsh ceffyl. Early forms and borrowing directions differ by word and remain disputed; this row does not make all three direct descendants of Latin caballus.
A Latin loan into Albanian: caballus → Proto-Albanian *kəβal → Albanian kalë.

English horse and Scots horse descend through Old English hors from Germanic *hrussą (also reconstructed *hursą). Proposed deeper derivations exist, including a connection with running, but are not certain. This is not *h₁éḱwos.

German Pferd, Dutch paard and Luxembourgish Päerd continue a borrowing of Late Latin paraverēdus, a substitute post horse. It combines Greek para- with Latin verēdus, a Gaulish loan. The whole word is not the ordinary inherited Germanic horse noun.

The Scandinavian hest/häst/hestur set descends from Germanic *hangistaz / *hanhistaz. West Frisian hynder is a compound based on the cognate hynst plus dier. Northern Sámi heasta and Greenlandic hiisti are Scandinavian borrowings. Their shared colour follows the word history rather than language family.

The selected Slavic konj/koń/kinʹ forms belong to the inherited Proto-Slavic horse set. Its deeper origin is debated, so no definite connection to the PIE *h₁éḱwos set is drawn. Russian also has конь; the common generic лошадь is selected separately.

Russian лошадь comes through Old East Slavic лоша from a Turkic source, compared with Tatar алаша and Chuvash лаша. The donor variety and deeper history are not fixed here. This set is distinct from Turkic at.
Lithuanian arklys is an agentive derivative connected with arklas, plough: a ploughing animal. It is not the same selected word as Latvian zirgs, although Lithuanian also has the cognate žirgas.
Latvian zirgs continues a Baltic horse word, cognate with Lithuanian žirgas. The map selects Lithuanian arklys separately rather than merging the two countries by family.

Breton marc’h and Cornish margh continue Celtic *markos. Its relationship to Germanic *marhaz and its deeper origin are debated. It is distinct from Celtic *ekwos, which survives in Scottish Gaelic each.

Modern Greek άλογο comes from the neuter of Ancient Greek ἄλογος, unreasoning or speechless, through its use for horse. Greek also has ίππος from the PIE horse word, but that is not the common label selected here.

Armenian ձի continues Old Armenian ji, compared with Vedic háya, horse, from a proposed Indo-European formation *ǵʰéyos associated with driving or impelling. It is kept separate from the regular *h₁éḱwos horse noun.

Romani grast, gras, gra and graj are cognate forms of an early Armenian loan. The selected Romanian grast and German Sinti graj share this origin colour. This is a distinct word history from Armenian dzi on the map. Different Romani varieties are not assumed to have unrelated horse nouns simply because they live in different countries.
Ossetian бӕх continues Alanic *bæx. Its deeper ancestry is unresolved here; belonging to Iranian does not make this noun a descendant of the asp/asb horse set.

Finnish hevonen and Estonian hobune continue diminutive formations of the Finnic horse word *hëpo; Karelian and Veps hebo continue the shorter form. A Germanic or other Indo-European source has been proposed, but no secure deeper link is asserted.

Hungarian ló (stem lov-), Khanty ԓов (Kazym łow, often simplified lov) and Northern Mansi лув (luw) share the inherited Ugric horse-word set. The Hungarian etymological dictionary reconstructs *luβɜ or *luγɜ. Its earlier donor and remote origin remain unresolved; no definite deeper Indo-European ancestry is asserted.
Udmurt вал and Komi вӧв are cognates continuing Permic *vɔ̇l, compared with a wider *wälɜ animal-word set. No direct connection with Hungarian ló or Finnic *hëpo is asserted.
Meadow Mari имне is cognate with Hill Mari имни. This attested Mari set is shown without an invented common Uralic horse root.

Tundra Nenets юно continues the Samoyedic *juntå horse set, traced to Old Turkic yunt. It is distinct from the Turkic at and yïlkï sets. Forest Nenets has a different Ugric loan; this map uses a Tundra Nenets reference.
Basque zaldi is an old Basque horse word. Its remote origin is not resolved by the present comparison and no shared PIE ancestry is asserted.

The selected Arabic citation form حصان means horse or stallion and belongs to the root ḥ-ṣ-n. It is distinct from the sus/susya set in Hebrew and Aramaic. Regional vowels vary; these labels are representative forms, not an inventory of all local synonyms.

Maghrebi Arabic عود is represented by Algerian ʿūd and Moroccan ʿawd. The proposed earlier Arabic sense is a camel trained for riding. Kossmann (2013, pp. 149–150) explicitly derives Kabyle aɛawḏiw / aɛudiw from Maghrebi Arabic ɛǝwd(a), so the Kabyle loan shares this origin colour. These are distinct from the ḥiṣān and faras horse-word sets.

The written Hassaniya horse word فرس is documented in the Peace Corps handbook, p. 249. It belongs to the Arabic faras horse-word set, distinct from ḥiṣān and ʿawd. The map uses frs as a consonant-only transliteration because the exact local vocalization has not been verified; it must not be read as an IPA pronunciation or silently replaced by the standard Arabic reading.

Hebrew sus and the selected Aramaic and Mandaic words belong to the old sūs/sūsyā horse-word set, also compared with Akkadian sīsû. Early borrowing and ultimate origins are disputed; they are not linked automatically to Arabic ḥiṣān or PIE *h₁éḱwos.
Maltese żiemel comes from Arabic zāmil, horse or wild ass, related to zāmila, a load-carrying she-camel. The semantic history involves a pack animal; this is not a reflex of the sus or ḥiṣān sets.

Central Atlas Tamazight ayis, Tachelhit ayyis and Rif yis belong to the inherited Berber horse-word set. Kossmann distinguishes them from Arabic-derived horse words and from the agmar set. No speculative remote Indo-European etymology is asserted.

Nafusi agmár and Ghadames aǧmar are members of the Berber GMR horse-word set, separate from ayis / yis and from Arabic horse loans. The comparison stops at this Berber set; a Latin or other remote origin is not asserted.
The at/ot set continues the Common Turkic horse word. Uzbek ot reflects the same set. Kazakh has at too, but the common species/livestock noun жылқы is selected separately.
Kazakh жылқы continues the Turkic yïlkï livestock/horse-herd term, related to the word for year or age in the cited analysis. It is a different lexical origin from at.
Georgian ცხენი continues Old Georgian ცხენი and is compared with Mingrelian and Laz forms in the Kartvelian *cxen- set. No PIE horse etymology is asserted.
Chechen and Ingush говр continue a Nakh horse-word set. The deeper history is not resolved here.
Adyghe and Kabardian шы continue the Circassian horse-word set. It is kept separate from the selected Northeast Caucasian words.
Avar чу is the documented horse noun. Proposed early Indo-Iranian connections in Caucasian horse terminology are not treated as settled by this map.

Dargwa урчи is the documented horse noun. An early Iranian source is proposed in the cited etymological material, but its chronology and relationship to neighbouring Caucasian words are left unresolved here.
Lezgian шив is an attested horse noun. Its remote relationship to other Caucasian and Iranian words is not established here.
Lak чву is an attested horse noun. It is shown as a local comparison set rather than assigned an unsupported deep ancestor.
Kalmyk мөрн in the horse sense continues Mongolic *morin. A homograph means river and has a different origin; that river etymology does not apply to this map.

Aleppo Domari agōra belongs to the inherited Indo-Aryan ghōṭa horse-word set documented by Herin. It is distinct from the Armenian grast loan found in Romani varieties, and is not assigned to the PIE h1ekwos set merely because Domari is Indo-European. Its more remote ancestry is not asserted.

g.text: Parentheses: romanized readings (frs: consonants only). * Reconstructed. “loan ?”: possible borrowing. Stripes: coexisting word origins; bars identify each. Dots: selected communities; hollow: word unverified. Romanian Romani census: >20% (2021). Areas generalized.
Areas: Asher & Moseley / DiACL / Rantanen via Glottography (CC BY 4.0); Romanian census supplements: INS RPL 2021 / ISPMN. Land: Natural Earth. Full sources: atlas data.
